query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is controlled by selective reactions at the grain boundaries—specifically, by localized oxidation (or reduction‐induced precipitation) of elements such as Cr and Ti that deplete these critical species from the matrix. This local elemental depletion leads to the formation of brittle phases (e.g., a sigma phase) and/or discontinuous, nonadherent intergranular oxides that weaken boundary cohesion, ultimately promoting rapid crack initiation and catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐manufactured HEA with an FCC matrix that is a supersaturated solid solution with a fairly uniform elemental distribution and minimal preexisting detrimental precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to isothermal exposures at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1000 °C) while systematically varying the gas environment – comparing high oxygen (oxidizing) conditions versus inert or mild reducing atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Expose samples at temperatures between approximately 800 and 1000 °C for prolonged durations (sufficient to activate diffusion processes) under controlled gas compositions (e.g., high oxygen partial pressures versus inert/reducing gases).
generation.structural_mediator: Intergranular features such as oxide scales or brittle precipitates (e.g., sigma phase) that form along grain boundaries as a result of selective reaction processes.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures enhance the diffusion of reactive species, so that in oxidizing atmospheres oxygen preferentially attacks more reactive elements (notably Cr and Ti) at the grain boundaries. This drives local compositional imbalance, promotes the nucleation of a brittle sigma phase and/or the formation of nonadherent oxide scales, and lowers intergranular cohesion. Under reducing or inert conditions, these processes are suppressed, preserving the structural integrity of the grain boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting state, specimens exposed to high-oxygen conditions will show thicker, possibly discontinuous oxide layers and/or increased sigma-phase precipitation at grain boundaries. These microstructural changes will correlate with reduced ductility and fracture toughness (evidenced by earlier crack initiation and rapid, catastrophic crack propagation) compared to specimens held in inert/reducing atmospheres.
generation.baseline: The initial as-manufactured state characterized by a uniform FCC solid solution with well-bonded grain boundaries and without significant grain-boundary segregations or secondary phase precipitates.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected in the temperature range of approximately 800–1000 °C and under gas exposures that provide a sufficient reactive potential (i.e., high oxygen partial pressure for oxidation or conversely for reduction-driven effects), with exposure durations long enough to permit diffusion-controlled processes.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thresholds for phase precipitation and oxide scale spallation are not fully quantified, and minor elements (for example, the role of Al) may modify kinetics somewhat; further quantification is needed to define exact exposure times and gas compositions necessary to trigger these processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple identical specimens of the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and expose them isothermally at 900 °C under two controlled atmospheres: one with a high oxygen partial pressure (oxidizing) and one with an inert or mildly reducing gas. After fixed exposure times, conduct thorough microstructural analyses (using TEM/SEM and EDS) to evaluate oxide layer thickness, grain boundary chemistry, and any formation of brittle precipitates. Perform mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) to assess changes in ductility and fracture toughness.
measurements: Grain boundary oxide or precipitate thickness and continuity (via microscopy)
Volume fraction and distribution of brittle phases (e.g., sigma phase) detected by phase analysis
Elemental segregation profiles at grain boundaries (using EDS or APT)
Mechanical properties such as tensile ductility and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens exposed to oxidizing conditions do not exhibit significantly greater intergranular oxidation or brittle precipitate formation—and these microstructural changes do not correlate with a measurable decrease in ductility and fracture toughness compared with specimens in inert/reducing conditions—then the hypothesis that selective grain-boundary reactions govern degradation and lead to catastrophic failure is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Al seems to have a minor effect on both Ni and Co, both of which are the weakest oxidizing component and it seems to have no effects on both unoxidized and oxidized states. We infer that Al addition does not have significant electronic interaction with Co and Ni (Fig. 4h, i), this is shown as their oxidation behavior remains the same in Fig. 4d. Figure 4j summarizes these interactions where Mn-Al tends to have the strongest interaction and both Ni and Co being the weakest. This study uncovers the oxidation process in compositionally complex alloys. Our study involved subjecting an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy to oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar oxygen pressure for both ex situ and in situ observations. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). We chose a relatively low oxidation temperature to prevent phase transformation in the alloy, focusing solely on examining the oxidation process in the super-saturated alloy condition.
